newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers to meet against backdrop of EMU row.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers to meet against backdrop of EMU row.

text.p: A Franco-German row over the merits of an informal economic council under monetary union is likely to simmer in the margins of Monday's ECOFIN Council meeting.

Although the official agenda for the Council is devoid of any substantive monetary issues, EU officials say France's determination to create a political counterweight to a future European Central Bank (ECB) could come up informally.
"I wouldn't fall off my chair with uncontrollable astonishment if (France) wanted to discuss the issue," commented one EU official on Friday.
Senior French finance ministry officials said earlier this week that their proposal for a Group of Seven-like council to discuss economic policy under a common currency could be raised on Monday.
The desire for such a grouping stems largely from France's fear that monetary policy under economic and monetary union (EMU) will be focused exclusively on fighting inflation.

With unemployment running at a double-digit pace in Europe and budgetary policies constrained by an agreed stability pact, there is worry that ECB policies based solely on price stability could undermine the prospects for robust economic growth.

France has worked hard to deny claims that it is seeking to politicise the ECB. But in Germany, where the future stability and credibility of the single currency is considered of paramount importance, criticism of such a council has risen to near fever pitch.
In a recent speech, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer stressed that the independence of the ECB is of "crucial importance" and must be protected from any political body.

"The Maastricht treaty has made this unmistakably clear. Various attempts to create a 'pouvoir politique' (political power) to control 'pouvoir monetaire' (monetary power) would not correspond to the Maastricht treaty," Tietmeyer said.
While few officials expect a flare-up in tensions between the two EU powers on Monday, the meeting could offer the first taste of the battle ahead.
Separately, there will an informal discussion of the meeting of G7 finance ministers and central bankers in Berlin on February 8.

Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt, in his capacity as Chairman of the International Monetary Fund's Interim Committee, will brief the ministers on the Berlin meeting. Diplomats said on Friday EMU will be among the items on the G7 agenda.

Another country to watch will be Britain. With Prime Minister John Major having adopted a harsher tone towards a common currency this week, all eyes will be on his Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke.
Major told parliament on Thursday that it was "very unlikely" sterling would join a single currency at the expected start date in 1999.
Until now, Clarke has argued that Britain had not ruled out the possiblity of entering EMU on time.
